Early rising: why your baby wakes so early and what to do first

Most early rising traces back to nap timing and total sleep pressure, not the room or a bad habit. Aim to have your baby out of the cot closer to 7 am; a wake between 6 and 7 am is not uncommon, but being up and done for the day well before 7 am is what is worth working on. Check first nap timing and the full sleep budget before changing anything else.

Written and reviewed by Sally Woods, internationally certified sleep consultant and former paediatric nurse. Last updated: August 27, 2026.

Is an early wake normal?

Usually normal

  • Waking between 6 and 7 am most days, rested and cheerful. Hold your 7 am start and set naps from there, not from the early wake.
  • Squirmy with eyes closed at 5:45 am, no crying yet. Wait 5 to 10 minutes before going in.

Worth working on

  • Wide awake and done at 5 am, tired and cranky by mid-morning. Review first nap timing and total sleep budget.
  • Wake time creeping 5 to 10 minutes earlier each week. Audit nap start times for gradual delays.

When to call your GP

  • Fever, feed refusal, pain or signs of dehydration. A baby under 3 months with a temperature of 38°C or higher needs urgent medical attention at the nearest emergency department. For an older baby with these signs, seek medical advice promptly.

First steps you can take today

  1. Check first nap timing. Compare your baby's first nap start to the wake window they can comfortably hold for their age. A first nap that drifts later than that window can pull the morning wake earlier.
  2. Add up the sleep budget. Total night sleep plus all naps. If the 24-hour figure sits under what your baby needs, the early wake is a sleep shortfall, not a habit, and the fix is more sleep during the day or an earlier bedtime.
  3. Test an earlier bedtime. If your baby shows over-tired signs like hard settling or fragmented nights, bring bedtime forward by 15 minutes and hold it for a week. More sleep pressure often pushes the morning wake later, not earlier.
  4. Log seven days first. Write down wake time, nap starts, nap lengths and bedtime for a week. Patterns show up in the log that daily memory misses, and later naps almost always sit before earlier wakes.

Why does my baby wake so early?

Early rising is a wake that starts the day too soon and will not settle back into real sleep, no matter what you try. A quick stir at 5 am that resolves in a few minutes is not early rising. A baby who is awake, alert and done for the day at 5 am is. A wake between 6 am and 7 am is not uncommon, and the aim is to have your baby out of the cot closer to 7 am. The wakes worth working on are the ones creeping earlier week by week, or leaving a baby up and done well before 7 am, tired and irritable by mid-morning.

Two things drive most early waking. Nap timing: when the first nap drifts later than the wake window your baby can hold, the whole day shifts and the morning wake creeps earlier. Total sleep budget: if the 24-hour sleep total sits under what your baby needs, they wake early because there is not enough sleep pressure to keep them asleep through to a normal wake time. On the consult floor, a common trap is blaming the room first. Parents buy heavier curtains before they look at nap timing. If the first nap has drifted later than the age-appropriate window, no amount of blackout fixes the wake until the timing is corrected.

Part of: Snooze › Sleep regressions

Sleep regressions: what they really are and what to do first

Most of what parents call a regression is really a schedule your baby has outgrown, or a new skill breaking through at night. The 4 month change is the exception: a permanent shift in how your baby sleeps, not a phase to wait out. Check the schedule first.

Written and reviewed by Sally Woods, internationally certified sleep consultant and former paediatric nurse. Last updated: August 27, 2026.

Is this a sleep regression?

Usually normal

  • Waking through the night again around 4 months, after a settled stretch. Treat it as a new baseline and steady the daytime rhythm.
  • Suddenly fighting or refusing a nap around 8 to 10 months. Give the skill plenty of practice in awake time and keep offering the nap.
  • Night wakings that started when a new motor skill did. Practise the skill during the day so nights feel less novel.
  • Screaming or stalling at bedtime around 18 months. Hold the routine and the limit calmly and consistently.

Worth working on

  • An early morning wake that appeared during a regression. Check the schedule before assuming the regression caused it.

When to call your GP

  • Fever, feed refusal, pain or signs of dehydration. A baby under 3 months with a temperature of 38°C or higher needs urgent medical attention at the nearest emergency department. For an older baby with these signs, seek medical advice promptly.

First steps you can take today

  1. Audit the schedule before you assume a regression. Overtiredness from a day that no longer fits is a common regression impostor, so check that first. If the wake windows that worked last month feel too short now, the day, not a phase, is the problem.
  2. Look for the developmental marker. A genuine regression usually pairs with a new skill: rolling, crawling, pulling up, first words or a fresh burst of separation awareness. Once you can spot the skill you can stop bracing and start supporting it.
  3. Log three to five days first. Note wake time, naps, feeds, night wakings and bedtime. A short log tells a true regression apart from a schedule that has slipped, which memory alone will miss.
  4. Rule out teething and illness. Sore gums and a cold can ride alongside a leap and muddy the picture. Check for fever, feed refusal or obvious pain before you pin everything on development.

What is a sleep regression really?

A regression is a real, temporary disruption to settled sleep that lines up with a burst of development. The catch is that most of what parents call a regression is not one: it is usually a schedule the baby has outgrown, or a new skill breaking through in the night. The 4 month change is the exception. It is the one true reset: around 4 months your baby's sleep cycles become more mature, with lighter phases between them, and that is permanent, not a phase to wait out.

Three things sit behind most regressions: an outgrown schedule, where wake windows that fit last month leave your baby overtired this month and overtiredness looks exactly like a regression; development, where a new motor skill, a language leap or separation awareness surfaces at night as your baby rehearses it; and the 4 month maturation, a permanent change in sleep architecture rather than a passing driver. On the consult floor, a common trap is a regression that turns out to be a schedule the baby quietly outgrew. That is why the first move is always to audit the schedule before you settle in to wait.

How sleep regressions differ by age

Regressions do not all behave the same way, so start with the one in front of you.

What changes around 4 months?

Sleep cycles mature and the wakes multiply. This is the one regression that is a permanent change rather than a phase, so it is worth meeting it with a plan.

What changes around 18 months and 2 years?

These two are behavioural as much as biological. Both turn on the schedule underneath them and the boundary you hold when it is tested.

Part of: Find the right sleep help › Catnapping

Catnapping: why your baby wakes after 20 minutes and what to do first

A catnap is a single sleep cycle that ends when your baby surfaces into light sleep and does not link into the next one. Short naps are completely normal in the early months and often need no fixing. A stuck 20 to 30 minute pattern in older babies is worth working on because it can chip away at night sleep.

Written and reviewed by Sally Woods, internationally certified sleep consultant and former paediatric nurse. Last updated: August 27, 2026.

Is catnapping normal?

Usually normal

  • Newborn catnaps through most of the day. Focus on safe sleep and feeding, not nap length.
  • Short naps during a known regression or nap transition. Hold your rhythm steady and wait it out.

Worth working on

  • Stuck 20 to 30 minute naps in an older baby who wakes cranky. Log naps and check total daytime sleep.
  • Catnapping alongside an early morning wake. Review nap timing across the whole day.

When to call your GP

  • Poor weight gain or feeding trouble. This is not a nap-length issue. Speak to your GP or child health nurse.

First steps you can take today

  1. Add up total daytime sleep. A baby who takes several short naps may be getting plenty of day sleep overall. Knowing the daily total tells you whether you are looking at a real shortfall or just a short-but-frequent napper.
  2. Check the tiredness fit. Note whether longer awake stretches make naps worse rather than better. If they do, an over-tired loop is the more likely driver than a baby who needs even more awake time.
  3. Log naps for a week. Write down when each nap started, how long it ran and how your baby woke. Patterns show up in the log that daily memory misses, and you will often see the short naps clustering around the same time of day.
  4. Rule out the obvious. Teething, illness, hunger and a nappy that needs changing all cut naps short. Clear these before you treat a run of short naps as a pattern to work on.

Why does my baby wake after a short nap?

A catnap is one sleep cycle. Baby drifts down into deep sleep, comes back up to the surface at the light-sleep join between cycles and then wakes fully instead of sliding into a second cycle. Short naps are not automatically a problem. In young babies they are simply how sleep is built, and a baby who catnaps but feeds well, grows well and is content between sleeps is doing fine. The pattern worth working on is a baby past the newborn stage who keeps cutting naps short, wakes cranky rather than rested and starts losing ground at night.

On the consult floor, a common trap is stretching wake windows to force a longer nap. It feels logical that a more tired baby should sleep longer, but it usually backfires and feeds an over-tired loop where naps get shorter rather than longer. More often the fix runs the other way. Easing the pressure before a nap tends to do more for the second sleep cycle than piling more onto it.

Catnapping FAQs

Quick answers parents ask when every nap ends at the 20 to 30 minute mark.

What is catnapping in babies?

Catnapping is when a nap ends after a single sleep cycle, often around 20 to 40 minutes, because your baby surfaces into light sleep and does not link into the next cycle. Short naps are common in young babies. A stuck short-nap pattern in an older baby who wakes cranky is the pattern worth working on.

Is a 20 minute nap normal?

Yes for many newborns and young babies, especially if they feed well, grow well and are content between sleeps. It is more of a concern when short naps drag on past the early months, leave your baby overtired, and start chipping away at night sleep.

Should I stretch wake windows to fix catnapping?

Usually not as the first move. Making a baby more tired to force a longer nap often backfires and feeds an over-tired loop. Easing pressure before the nap and checking the whole day's timing tends to help more than piling on awake time.

Can catnapping cause early rising or night wakes?

It can. When daytime sleep is fragmented, overnight sleep often fragments too. If short naps travel with early mornings, review nap timing across the whole day rather than treating the morning wake in isolation. See our early rising guide as well.

What should I try first for short naps?

Log naps for a week, add up total daytime sleep, check whether longer awake stretches make naps worse, and rule out teething, illness, hunger or a wet nappy. Those four steps tell you whether you are looking at a normal young-baby pattern or a stuck loop to work on.

When should I get more help for catnapping?

If your baby is past the newborn stage, short naps are stuck, nights are suffering, and the first steps are not shifting things, it is reasonable to use a fuller plan and support. Poor weight gain or feeding trouble is not a nap-length issue, speak to your GP or child health nurse. For sleep planning support, explore the Snooze membership.
